It's an owner-triggered command; the mechanics — which files to edit and how a release follows — live in the consuming project's workflow doc. - **"Show me the document"** (for a source-controlled document) is the owner's phrase asking for a **link to the document on GitHub** — not the file's contents inlined, and not a local filesystem path. When the document lives in a GitHub-hosted repo, respond with a GitHub link to it (the file on the relevant branch/commit); only fall back to inlining the contents or giving a local path when the document isn't under source control. - **Put decisions and approvals in an `AskUserQuestion` popup, not buried in prose.** The owner is frequently on mobile, where a popup notifies and a question embedded in a paragraph is easy to miss. When you need the owner to choose or approve something, ask through the structured popup with explicit options rather than asking in running text. **And when several independent items each need a verdict** (a set of proposed fixes, findings to accept), give **each item its own question carrying its own brief case** — the concrete failure, why it matters, the cost of the fix — with per-item approve/defer options; never one bundled choose-a-scope question over the whole set. The owner decides item-wise, from the case, not from a menu of subsets. (The popup carries at most 4 questions per call — split a larger set into consecutive calls.) - **When asked to produce a prompt or message destined for another context, visually enclose the whole thing.** Any text the owner will lift out and use elsewhere — a prompt for another assistant, a message to send, copy meant to be pasted somewhere — must be set apart as a single delimited block: either a box (e.g. a fenced code block) or fenced top and bottom by two separating lines, so its exact boundaries are unmistakable and it can be copied in one piece. This composes with the enclose-the-whole-thing preference above: the disclaimer sits inside the same delimited block as the prompt it prefixes. - **Auto-open a PR after committing.** Whenever Claude changes code on a branch and commits it, open a pull request for that branch right after, even without an explicit request to do so. This overrides Claude Code's own default of only opening a PR when explicitly asked. # Claudinite — active-pack guidance The baseline plus the packs this project declares. Deeper per-pack reference (e.g. a pack's release doc) is linked from its prose and read on demand. # Working discipline The working discipline that isn't itself a GitHub operation — general habits for how to approach a change, independent of any one project. Start every requested change from the *problem*, not the solution — in any repository, not just this one. Before implementing, reach an explicit shared understanding with the owner of the problem the change is meant to solve **and** agreement that the requested change is the best way to solve it; a different fix, or no change at all, may serve the underlying problem better. Open your reply to an owner comment with an explicit classification line — `Comment class: correction | feature | process-change | other` (`other` covers questions, approvals, and command phrases; a mixed comment names each part). The class decides where the change lands and what must exist before any fix. 1. **A correction** — you misunderstood something. Repair the shared understanding, then rework what the misread already touched; the artifact changes as much as the correction demands, but a correction never adds a new requirement or rule. 2. **A feature** — agree on the requirement, record it in the project's requirements document (its executable spec, where it keeps one), write the test that proves it and watch it fail, then implement until it passes. 3. **A process change** — the owner is changing *how* work is done. The change lands as durable rules in the project's local scope — its own local packs (in Claudinite itself, its packs) — routed through the mechanism promotion ladder (platform setting → hook → check → skill → prose); promoting a rule into the shared canon is the growth lifecycle's separate call, not the interactive session's. Author the assurance first — the check the future world must satisfy — execute it and watch it fail, and only then make the fixes that turn it green. When the ladder lands the rule at prose (an in-flight judgment rule no check can carry), the equivalent step is showing the corpus doesn't already cover the rule before writing it. The two build modes share one spine: state the expectation in its durable home first, watch it fail against the current world, then change the world to satisfy it — a fix made before its assurance exists can never show it addressed what the owner actually asked for. Before building a mechanism for a behavior, verify against a real run that it isn't already provided. When feedback flags a misunderstanding, check whether the artifact is already correct before expanding it — if it is, say so and push back rather than editing; a misread doesn't imply the text is wrong. And size writing to its idea: "open one issue" takes a sentence, not three paragraphs. When correcting or auditing an artifact against an authoritative source, derive the corrected version from the *source* before reading the existing draft, then diff against the old draft to surface what was actually wrong — reading the draft first anchors you to its framing and quietly carries its errors into your "fix." Fix build/test/CI warnings rather than tolerating them, with a small, targeted fix that addresses the *cause* in the same change — a clean run makes a genuinely new warning or error stand out. Suppressing a warning — muting it with a flag (e.g. `--disable-warning`), `eslint-disable`, swallowing it, etc. — is **not** a small fix and never the quick path: reach for it only as a deliberate, reviewed decision once the real fix has been weighed and rejected. A suppression you do keep must **carry its reason at the site**: on the suppression line, or in the comment immediately above it, saying why the fix was rejected — that inline reason *is* the review record, so no second justification is recorded elsewhere. Before working around a finding from a vendored check, confirm the vendored copy is current — it reflects its last refresh, not upstream's head, so the fix may already exist upstream and simply not be pulled in yet. When a warning can't be fixed with a small cause-addressing change now without hindering current work (e.g. it's waiting on an upstream release, or the real fix is a larger refactor), open a dedicated issue for it unless one is already open, then move on — resolving it (real fix, or a consciously-chosen suppression) happens in that issue's own change. An approval — to merge, to ship, to proceed — applies only *backward*, to the work already in front of the owner when it's given, never to anything requested or done *after* it. A later follow-up, even a fix to the just-approved change, needs its own explicit approval; a chosen answer to a multiple-choice prompt isn't authorization just because an option's wording mentioned the action. # The task lifecycle The issue → branch → PR lifecycle every new task follows, independent of any one project. The rest of the git/GitHub procedures live in the `git-github-advanced` skill. For every new task: 1. Create a GitHub issue describing the task before starting work. 2. Develop on a branch; reference that issue number in commit messages (e.g. `Refs #123`, `Fixes #123`, or `Closes #123`). 3. Update the issue's status (comments / close) as work progresses and when it's done. --- # HTML Portable, project-agnostic practices for hand-authored HTML — semantic markup, accessibility, forms, and the document structure pitfalls that recur regardless of framework — true for any HTML read cold. - **Injected block markup inside a `

` right before it and the injected content lands as the `

Reserve "test it after it's deployed" for behavior you've verified genuinely can't be observed now. - **Make that console request a snippet, not an essay.** Send exactly one code block to paste into the console and ask the user to paste its output back. The repo's own scheduler runs the pack's three maintenance tasks — `tidy-issues`, `tidy-prs`, `tidy-branches`, one per dimension; this is the policy they follow. Judge by *content* (the landed-status test), never a ref's auto-generated name. - **Issues — act.** Take the first applicable action: close-if-implemented / needs-decision / blocked / quick-win / leave. Every action defaults to the reversible option (comment / leave) when the check is inconclusive. Each task applies its single-object skill across the targets its precondition hands it, then rewrites **its own** standing tracker from the verdicts it gathered (one issue per dimension per repo, body rewritten to today's state, a dated comment per run). ## github
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. Query strings should contain only search criteria (e.g., 'org:google language:python'), not sorting instructions. Always call 'get_me' first to understand current user permissions and context. ## Issues

Check 'list_issue_types' first for organizations to use proper issue types. Use 'search_issues' before creating new issues to avoid duplicates. Always set 'state_reason' when closing issues. ## Pull Requests

PR review workflow: Always use 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'create' to create a pending review, then 'add_comment_to_pending_review' to add comments, and finally 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'submit_pending' to submit the review for complex reviews with line-specific comments.

Before creating a pull request, search for pull request templates in the repository. Template files are called pull_request_template.md or they're located in '.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE' directory. Use the template content to structure the PR description and then call create_pull_request tool.

=== generate-project-instructions SKILL.md ===
---
name: generate-project-instructions
description: Decompose a project into its pack facets (working-style class, technology, aspect, domain) and extract its working instructions into reusable canon packs plus the project's own local packs (.claudinite/local_packs/). Use when a project has no established working style yet, or it exhibits a facet no pack covers — during bootstrap of a fresh/empty repo, or on an uplevel request.
---

# Generate project instructions — extract packs, not a project doc

This skill grows the corpus's pack library using the project in front of you as the evidence, and
lands the project's own working rules where every project's do now: its **local packs**. The owner's
projects recur — not as wholes, but **along axes**: the same working style returns with a different
product, the same technology returns with a different working style, the same audience returns on a
different stack. The first project to exhibit a facet pays the cost of working out how that facet is
handled; a **canon** pack is how every later project sharing it starts from the answer instead of
re-deriving it — and what stays specific to *this* project lands in **its own local pack**, the same
pack machinery run from the project's tree.

The deliverable is therefore **two kinds of pack**, never a single "how to work on this repo" document:

- **Canon pack seeds and refinements** — one `packs/<facet>/` per facet where this project has real
  portable insight, each written as if this project didn't exist, proposed to Claudinite.
- **The project's own local pack(s)** — under `.claudinite/local_packs/<pack>/` in the project's tree:
  the project-specific working style, concrete values (real commands, paths, names, metrics), and the
  project-specific rules that *don't* generalize — carried the same way any pack carries them (a check
  in the pack's `rules`, an activity skill, prose in `RULES.md`, a scheduled task), not a thin doc.
  This is the project's normalized capture surface; its `CLAUDE.md` is a thin routing map to it, loaded
  through the pack system rather than `@import`.

The failure mode this skill exists to prevent: investigating the repo and producing one competent "how
to work on this repo" document — real commands, real paths, this product's concepts — with the
reusable core never separated out and the project-specific core dumped as always-loaded prose. If
portable guidance ends up in a local pack (it should be a canon pack), or the project's file names end
up in a canon pack (they belong in the local pack), the split is wrong.

## 1. Gather the evidence

Read the project before writing a word: README and existing docs, `CLAUDE.md` and everything it
imports, dependency and build manifests, scripts and CI, the test layout, git history and recent
PRs/issues, and any conversation with the owner about how they want to work. You are collecting two
things, both grounded in what you actually find:

- the **facets** this project exhibits (step 2), and
- every **candidate rule** — each convention, procedure, or quality bar the project works by — ready to
  be sorted by owner (step 3).

Invent nothing. If a call that changes the outcome is genuinely open, ask the owner one focused
question (via the structured popup); otherwise take the sensible default and note it.

## 2. Decompose into facets, and check the shelf per facet

A project is a bundle of **facets**, each a candidate pack on its own axis:

- **Class — the working style.** How work runs end to end: the loop by which a change is proposed,
  verified, and shipped; the production bar; audience and longevity. Test: the pack still fits a
  project on a different stack, for a different product idea.
- **Technology — the platform.** True for any project on that platform, whatever its class or product.
  Test: the pack still fits when the product and the working style change. The first project on a new
  platform mints its pack — an iPhone app arriving tomorrow mints `iphone-app` the same way
  `chrome-extension` and `aws-sam` were minted.
- **Aspect — a separable slice of concern**, usually with its own on-switch. `chrome-extension-release`
  is the same technology as `chrome-extension` at a different moment: the release/store standard a
  project declares only once it ships. Split an aspect out of its parent facet when its rules activate
  at a different time or under a different decision than the parent's.
- **Domain — the audience or setting**, when it changes how work is done. A children's-app pack would
  carry design-review, requirement-processing, and compliance rules that hold whether the app is
  Flutter or web; a regulated-industry pack likewise. A domain that doesn't change the working rules
  isn't a facet worth a pack.

**The product itself is never a facet** — "this specific product" doesn't recur, by definition; its
rules land in the project's own local pack.

And a *statement of what the product does* isn't a pack rule at all — not even a local one. A pack, canon
or local, homes **how we work**: the conventions, gotchas and review discipline that recur across tasks
whatever the feature happens to be. A rule asserting which entities exist, what a surface must render, or
that a feature's parts are wired to each other is a **requirement**; its home is the project's executable
spec and the suite that proves it. Encoding it as a pack check instead splits one feature's definition
across two systems and lands it in the one no test of the product ever reads. Pack-worthiness is a question
about the *work*, not about how load-bearing the code is — a real gap in product coverage is a requirements
gap, and answering it with a pack is how a feature's spec ends up somewhere nothing executes it.

<example>
One extension project can exhibit four facets at once: `spec-driven-product` (class),
`chrome-extension` + `node` (technologies), `chrome-extension-release` (aspect, once it ships) — and
its local pack holds only what none of them own.
</example>

Then check the canon shelf **per facet** (`packs/` here; the mounted `.claudinite/packs/` in a

1	---
2	name: generate-project-instructions
3	description: Decompose a project into its pack facets (working-style class, technology, aspect, domain) and extract its working instructions into reusable canon packs plus the project's own local packs (.claudinite/local_packs/). Use when a project has no established working style yet, or it exhibits a facet no pack covers — during bootstrap of a fresh/empty repo, or on an uplevel request.
4	---
5	
6	# Generate project instructions — extract packs, not a project doc
7	
8	This skill grows the corpus's pack library using the project in front of you as the evidence, and
9	lands the project's own working rules where every project's do now: its **local packs**. The owner's
10	projects recur — not as wholes, but **along axes**: the same working style returns with a different
11	product, the same technology returns with a different working style, the same audience returns on a
12	different stack. The first project to exhibit a facet pays the cost of working out how that facet is
13	handled; a **canon** pack is how every later project sharing it starts from the answer instead of
14	re-deriving it — and what stays specific to *this* project lands in **its own local pack**, the same
15	pack machinery run from the project's tree.
16	
17	The deliverable is therefore **two kinds of pack**, never a single "how to work on this repo" document:
18	
19	- **Canon pack seeds and refinements** — one `packs/<facet>/` per facet where this project has real
20	  portable insight, each written as if this project didn't exist, proposed to Claudinite.
21	- **The project's own local pack(s)** — under `.claudinite/local_packs/<pack>/` in the project's tree:
22	  the project-specific working style, concrete values (real commands, paths, names, metrics), and the
23	  project-specific rules that *don't* generalize — carried the same way any pack carries them (a check
24	  in the pack's `rules`, an activity skill, prose in `RULES.md`, a scheduled task), not a thin doc.
25	  This is the project's normalized capture surface; its `CLAUDE.md` is a thin routing map to it, loaded
26	  through the pack system rather than `@import`.
27	
28	The failure mode this skill exists to prevent: investigating the repo and producing one competent "how
29	to work on this repo" document — real commands, real paths, this product's concepts — with the
30	reusable core never separated out and the project-specific core dumped as always-loaded prose. If
31	portable guidance ends up in a local pack (it should be a canon pack), or the project's file names end
32	up in a canon pack (they belong in the local pack), the split is wrong.
33	
34	## 1. Gather the evidence
35	
36	Read the project before writing a word: README and existing docs, `CLAUDE.md` and everything it
37	imports, dependency and build manifests, scripts and CI, the test layout, git history and recent
38	PRs/issues, and any conversation with the owner about how they want to work. You are collecting two
39	things, both grounded in what you actually find:
40	
41	- the **facets** this project exhibits (step 2), and
42	- every **candidate rule** — each convention, procedure, or quality bar the project works by — ready to
43	  be sorted by owner (step 3).
44	
45	Invent nothing. If a call that changes the outcome is genuinely open, ask the owner one focused
46	question (via the structured popup); otherwise take the sensible default and note it.
47	
48	## 2. Decompose into facets, and check the shelf per facet
49	
50	A project is a bundle of **facets**, each a candidate pack on its own axis:
51	
52	- **Class — the working style.** How work runs end to end: the loop by which a change is proposed,
53	  verified, and shipped; the production bar; audience and longevity. Test: the pack still fits a
54	  project on a different stack, for a different product idea.
55	- **Technology — the platform.** True for any project on that platform, whatever its class or product.
56	  Test: the pack still fits when the product and the working style change. The first project on a new
57	  platform mints its pack — an iPhone app arriving tomorrow mints `iphone-app` the same way
58	  `chrome-extension` and `aws-sam` were minted.
59	- **Aspect — a separable slice of concern**, usually with its own on-switch. `chrome-extension-release`
60	  is the same technology as `chrome-extension` at a different moment: the release/store standard a
61	  project declares only once it ships. Split an aspect out of its parent facet when its rules activate
62	  at a different time or under a different decision than the parent's.
63	- **Domain — the audience or setting**, when it changes how work is done. A children's-app pack would
64	  carry design-review, requirement-processing, and compliance rules that hold whether the app is
65	  Flutter or web; a regulated-industry pack likewise. A domain that doesn't change the working rules
66	  isn't a facet worth a pack.
67	
68	**The product itself is never a facet** — "this specific product" doesn't recur, by definition; its
69	rules land in the project's own local pack.
70	
71	And a *statement of what the product does* isn't a pack rule at all — not even a local one. A pack, canon
72	or local, homes **how we work**: the conventions, gotchas and review discipline that recur across tasks
73	whatever the feature happens to be. A rule asserting which entities exist, what a surface must render, or
74	that a feature's parts are wired to each other is a **requirement**; its home is the project's executable
75	spec and the suite that proves it. Encoding it as a pack check instead splits one feature's definition
76	across two systems and lands it in the one no test of the product ever reads. Pack-worthiness is a question
77	about the *work*, not about how load-bearing the code is — a real gap in product coverage is a requirements
78	gap, and answering it with a pack is how a feature's spec ends up somewhere nothing executes it.
79	
80	<example>
81	One extension project can exhibit four facets at once: `spec-driven-product` (class),
82	`chrome-extension` + `node` (technologies), `chrome-extension-release` (aspect, once it ships) — and
83	its local pack holds only what none of them own.
84	</example>
85	
86	Then check the canon shelf **per facet** (`packs/` here; the mounted `.claudinite/packs/` in a
87	consuming repo — a facet already owned by a *canon* pack is declared, not re-authored locally):
88	
89	- **Covered** → declare it (technology facets are usually already declared from the fingerprint) and
90	  move on — unless this project's evidence **sharpens or contradicts** the pack, which becomes a
91	  refinement PR to that pack, not a fork. Each further project of a facet is another exemplar: the
92	  pack should read as the intersection-plus-union of all of them, and a rule only one exemplar
93	  supports should say so or wait.
94	- **Uncovered, with real portable insight in the evidence** → this skill mints it (steps 3–4).
95	- **Uncovered, but this project has nothing durable to say about it yet** → leave it; a pack of
96	  placeholders helps nobody.
97	
98	Write each facet down — a short name plus one defining sentence — before drafting anything; every
99	sorting decision in step 3 tests against them.
100	
101	## 3. Sort every candidate rule to the single facet that owns it
102	
103	For each rule from step 1, apply the **portability strip per facet**: delete from the rule everything
104	the facet doesn't keep, and see whether something meaningful survives.
105	
106	- Delete the product and the stack, keep the loop — survives? → the **class** pack (canon).
107	- Delete the product and the working style, keep the platform — survives? → the **technology** (or
108	  **aspect**) pack (canon).
109	- Delete the stack, keep the audience/setting — survives? → the **domain** pack (canon).
110	- Survives nothing → project-specific: the project's **own local pack**.
111	
112	Route each rule to **exactly one owner** — the facet whose whole population the rule serves. "True for
113	any Node service" belongs to the canon `node` pack, not to this project's class pack, even if every
114	project of the class happens to use Node. Rewrite what lands in a canon pack project-agnostically and
115	parameterized, the way research-project does ("read *input* as whatever it means for your project").
116	
117	Then gate **every** pack-bound rule — canon or local — on the promotion ladder
118	([engine/checks/DESIGN.md](../../../../engine/checks/DESIGN.md)): a rule a deterministic **check** could enforce, or a
119	procedure with a nameable trigger a **skill** could carry, becomes that (in a canon seed it's flagged
120	as a check/skill candidate; in a local pack you author the check outright in the pack's `rules`, with
121	a red-first fixture) rather than settling as prose. What remains in a `RULES.md` is the always-relevant
122	judgment core of its facet — write more checks and less prose. Dedupe against the corpus: a rule the
123	basics baseline, an existing canon pack, or a skill already owns is not pack material at all.
124	
125	## 4. Write each pack
126	
127	Mint a pack for a facet only when its surviving rules clear the bar — several durable rules, not one
128	stray (a single rule joins the nearest existing pack, or waits as a handoff note). Each
129	`packs/<facet>/` needs four things (mirror `research-project/` and `chrome-extension/`):
130	
131	- **`RULES.md`** — the playbook, addressed to the *next* project sharing the facet, on day one. Open
132	  with the facet's one-line definition and "a default to adapt, not a contract". Principle-first, each
133	  rule carrying its why. It loads at session start for every declaring project, so every line pays
134	  rent — cover the facet, not everything you noticed.
135	- **`pack.mjs`** — the manifest. Class/domain/aspect packs: `always: false`, `marker: null`,
136	  `detect: null` (declaration is authoritative). Technology packs: add the `marker`/`detect`
137	  fingerprint when the repo carries a reliable one, so `--init` seeds the pack into a fresh
138	  declaration; the marker only *suspects* a pack is wanted, it never forces its declaration.
139	  Discovery is structural — the directory is the registration.
140	- **`README.md`** — the pack's rule table (section ≤5 words | how enforced), plus one provenance line
141	  naming the project it was distilled from.
142	- **Index entries** — a row in [packs/README.md](../../../../packs/README.md) and, for a new pack kind, the
143	  matching line in the corpus map ([README.md](../../../../README.md) — there is no agent-facing corpus index, #385).
144	
145	The acid test before proposing any pack: **a reader must not be able to tell which project it was
146	extracted from.** Any surviving repo path, command line, or product noun marks a rule that belonged in
147	the overlay.
148	
149	## 5. Write the project's own local pack(s)
150	
151	The project-specific residue lands in a **local pack** under `.claudinite/local_packs/<pack>/` in the
152	project's tree — the same pack machinery, run from the project instead of the canon. Most projects
153	need **one** general pack (name it for the project); segregate a **second** only when a distinct domain
154	earns its own bundle (the way the reference project split a general working pack from an
155	extractor-automation pack). Each local pack is a real pack:
156	
157	- **`pack.mjs`** — `{ id, detect: null, marker: null, prose: 'RULES.md', rules: [...], skills: [...] }`.
158	  A local pack is declared by hand, never fingerprinted or seeded (`detect`/`marker` stay null), as its
159	  namespaced token `local_packs/<name>` in `.claudinite-checks.json`; its id
160	  must be unique and may not shadow a canon pack.
161	- **`RULES.md`** — the always-loaded judgment core and the project's concrete values (real
162	  setup/run/verify commands, real paths, inputs, metrics, invariants). Keep it terse; anything a check
163	  or skill can carry doesn't belong here, and anything inferable from the code is omitted.
164	- **Checks** (`rules`) — the project-specific deterministic rules as `.mjs` modules listed on
165	  `pack.mjs`, each with a red-first fixture (`pack.test.mjs`) runnable by the project's own test suite.
166	  Local check modules stay dependency-free (they must load without the gitignored mount): return plain
167	  finding objects rather than importing the engine's helpers.
168	- **Skills** (`skills/<name>/SKILL.md`) — the project's activity-scoped procedures, bundled in the pack;
169	  a local pack may also *require* a canon skill by name.
170	- **Scheduled tasks** (`tasks/<name>/task.mjs` + its `task.md`) — first-class like every other slot:
171	  the repo's own scheduler discovers a local pack's tasks in the same scan that finds a canon pack's,
172	  gated by the project's declaration exactly the same way. So project-specific scheduled work belongs
173	  in a local task declaration (a self-contained module honoring the task contract, with its
174	  co-located worker doc), not an out-of-repo routine and not a cron of its own.
175	
176	The project's `CLAUDE.md` becomes a thin **routing map** to its local packs (and its genuine design
177	docs) — it does **not** `@import` the pack prose; the pack system injects the active local packs'
178	`RULES.md` at session start, the same as the canon packs'.
179	
180	## 6. Deliver through the owner's approval gates
181	
182	- **Every canon pack seed or refinement → a PR against Claudinite.** Minting or changing a *canon* pack
183	  is the owner's call, and the PR is that gate — no corpus change lands unattended
184	  ([the canon-curation README](../../../../.claudinite/local/packs/canon-curation/README.md)). From a consuming repo, never edit the read-only
185	  `.claudinite/` mount: open the Claudinite PR when the session can reach that repo; otherwise stage the
186	  seed as a **local pack** clearly marked as a proposed-canon facet and open a Claudinite issue pointing
187	  at it, so the promote stage lifts it centrally.
188	- **The project's local pack(s) → the project's normal branch/PR**, committed under
189	  `.claudinite/local_packs/` (tracked project content — the sync hook preserves it, the gitignore
190	  re-includes it). Declaring a **local** pack — as `local_packs/<name>` — is valid immediately (the
191	  engine discovers local packs from the repo), so the declaration lands in the same PR.
192	- **Declare a new *canon* pack** in `.claudinite-checks.json` only after it has merged and the mount
193	  re-synced — declaring a canon id the mounted registry doesn't know is an unknown-pack settings error;
194	  a *local* id is never that error. Note a pending canon declaration as a follow-up in the project PR.
195	- **Existing projects sharing a facet keep their local packs for now.** Once the canon pack lands, the
196	  growth dedup stage prunes what the canon newly owns; don't pre-trim against an unmerged pack.
197	
198	Close with a short report: each facet and its one-line definition, with its shelf verdict (declared /
199	refined / minted-to-canon / kept-local / left alone); the sort tally (rules sent to each canon pack /
200	the local pack / as a check vs. a skill vs. prose); and links to the PRs.

## 2. Decompose into facets, and check the shelf per facet

A project is a bundle of **facets**, each a candidate pack on its own axis:

- **Class — the working style.** How work runs end to end: the loop by which a change is proposed,
  verified, and shipped; the production bar; audience and longevity. Test: the pack still fits a
  project on a different stack, for a different product idea.
- **Technology — the platform.** True for any project on that platform, whatever its class or product.
  Test: the pack still fits when the product and the working style change. The first project on a new
  platform mints its pack — an iPhone app arriving tomorrow mints `iphone-app` the same way
  `chrome-extension` and `aws-sam` were minted.
- **Aspect — a separable slice of concern**, usually with its own on-switch. `chrome-extension-release`
  is the same technology as `chrome-extension` at a different moment: the release/store standard a
  project declares only once it ships. Split an aspect out of its parent facet when its rules activate
  at a different time or under a different decision than the parent's.
- **Domain — the audience or setting**, when it changes how work is done. A children's-app pack would
  carry design-review, requirement-processing, and compliance rules that hold whether the app is
  Flutter or web; a regulated-industry pack likewise. A domain that doesn't change the working rules
  isn't a facet worth a pack.

**The product itself is never a facet** — "this specific product" doesn't recur, by definition; its
rules land in the project's own local pack.

And a *statement of what the product does* isn't a pack rule at all — not even a local one. A pack, canon
or local, homes **how we work**: the conventions, gotchas and review discipline that recur across tasks
whatever the feature happens to be. A rule asserting which entities exist, what a surface must render, or
that a feature's parts are wired to each other is a **requirement**; its home is the project's executable
spec and the suite that proves it. Encoding it as a pack check instead splits one feature's definition
across two systems and lands it in the one no test of the product ever reads. Pack-worthiness is a question
about the *work*, not about how load-bearing the code is — a real gap in product coverage is a requirements
gap, and answering it with a pack is how a feature's spec ends up somewhere nothing executes it.

<example>
One extension project can exhibit four facets at once: `spec-driven-product` (class),
`chrome-extension` + `node` (technologies), `chrome-extension-release` (aspect, once it ships) — and
its local pack holds only what none of them own.
</example>

Then check the canon shelf **per facet** (`packs/` here; the mounted `.claudinite/packs/` in a
consuming repo — a facet already owned by a *canon* pack is declared, not re-authored locally):

- **Covered** → declare it (technology facets are usually already declared from the fingerprint) and
  move on — unless this project's evidence **sharpens or contradicts** the pack, which becomes a
  refinement PR to that pack, not a fork. Each further project of a facet is another exemplar: the
  pack should read as the intersection-plus-union of all of them, and a rule only one exemplar
  supports should say so or wait.
- **Uncovered, with real portable insight in the evidence** → this skill mints it (steps 3–4).
- **Uncovered, but this project has nothing durable to say about it yet** → leave it; a pack of
  placeholders helps nobody.

Write each facet down — a short name plus one defining sentence — before drafting anything; every
sorting decision in step 3 tests against them.

## 3. Sort every candidate rule to the single facet that owns it

For each rule from step 1, apply the **portability strip per facet**: delete from the rule everything
the facet doesn't keep, and see whether something meaningful survives.

- Delete the product and the stack, keep the loop — survives? → the **class** pack (canon).
- Delete the product and the working style, keep the platform — survives? → the **technology** (or
  **aspect**) pack (canon).
- Delete the stack, keep the audience/setting — survives? → the **domain** pack (canon).
- Survives nothing → project-specific: the project's **own local pack**.

Route each rule to **exactly one owner** — the facet whose whole population the rule serves. "True for
any Node service" belongs to the canon `node` pack, not to this project's class pack, even if every
project of the class happens to use Node. Rewrite what lands in a canon pack project-agnostically and
parameterized, the way research-project does ("read *input* as whatever it means for your project").

Then gate **every** pack-bound rule — canon or local — on the promotion ladder
([engine/checks/DESIGN.md](../../../../engine/checks/DESIGN.md)): a rule a deterministic **check** could enforce, or a
procedure with a nameable trigger a **skill** could carry, becomes that (in a canon seed it's flagged
as a check/skill candidate; in a local pack you author the check outright in the pack's `rules`, with
a red-first fixture) rather than settling as prose. What remains in a `RULES.md` is the always-relevant
judgment core of its facet — write more checks and less prose. Dedupe against the corpus: a rule the
basics baseline, an existing canon pack, or a skill already owns is not pack material at all.

## 4. Write each pack

Mint a pack for a facet only when its surviving rules clear the bar — several durable rules, not one
stray (a single rule joins the nearest existing pack, or waits as a handoff note). Each
`packs/<facet>/` needs four things (mirror `research-project/` and `chrome-extension/`):

- **`RULES.md`** — the playbook, addressed to the *next* project sharing the facet, on day one. Open
  with the facet's one-line definition and "a default to adapt, not a contract". Principle-first, each
  rule carrying its why. It loads at session start for every declaring project, so every line pays
  rent — cover the facet, not everything you noticed.
- **`pack.mjs`** — the manifest. Class/domain/aspect packs: `always: false`, `marker: null`,
  `detect: null` (declaration is authoritative). Technology packs: add the `marker`/`detect`
  fingerprint when the repo carries a reliable one, so `--init` seeds the pack into a fresh
  declaration; the marker only *suspects* a pack is wanted, it never forces its declaration.
  Discovery is structural — the directory is the registration.
- **`README.md`** — the pack's rule table (section ≤5 words | how enforced), plus one provenance line
  naming the project it was distilled from.
- **Index entries** — a row in [packs/README.md](../../../../packs/README.md) and, for a new pack kind, the
  matching line in the corpus map ([README.md](../../../../README.md) — there is no agent-facing corpus index, #385).

The acid test before proposing any pack: **a reader must not be able to tell which project it was
extracted from.** Any surviving repo path, command line, or product noun marks a rule that belonged in
the overlay.

## 5. Write the project's own local pack(s)

The project-specific residue lands in a **local pack** under `.claudinite/local_packs/<pack>/` in the
project's tree — the same pack machinery, run from the project instead of the canon. Most projects
need **one** general pack (name it for the project); segregate a **second** only when a distinct domain
earns its own bundle (the way the reference project split a general working pack from an
extractor-automation pack). Each local pack is a real pack:

- **`pack.mjs`** — `{ id, detect: null, marker: null, prose: 'RULES.md', rules: [...], skills: [...] }`.
  A local pack is declared by hand, never fingerprinted or seeded (`detect`/`marker` stay null), as its
  namespaced token `local_packs/<name>` in `.claudinite-checks.json`; its id
  must be unique and may not shadow a canon pack.
- **`RULES.md`** — the always-loaded judgment core and the project's concrete values (real
  setup/run/verify commands, real paths, inputs, metrics, invariants). Keep it terse; anything a check
  or skill can carry doesn't belong here, and anything inferable from the code is omitted.
- **Checks** (`rules`) — the project-specific deterministic rules as `.mjs` modules listed on
  `pack.mjs`, each with a red-first fixture (`pack.test.mjs`) runnable by the project's own test suite.
  Local check modules stay dependency-free (they must load without the gitignored mount): return plain
  finding objects rather than importing the engine's helpers.
- **Skills** (`skills/<name>/SKILL.md`) — the project's activity-scoped procedures, bundled in the pack;
  a local pack may also *require* a canon skill by name.
- **Scheduled tasks** (`tasks/<name>/task.mjs` + its `task.md`) — first-class like every other slot:
  the repo's own scheduler discovers a local pack's tasks in the same scan that finds a canon pack's,
  gated by the project's declaration exactly the same way. So project-specific scheduled work belongs
  in a local task declaration (a self-contained module honoring the task contract, with its
  co-located worker doc), not an out-of-repo routine and not a cron of its own.

The project's `CLAUDE.md` becomes a thin **routing map** to its local packs (and its genuine design
docs) — it does **not** `@import` the pack prose; the pack system injects the active local packs'
`RULES.md` at session start, the same as the canon packs'.

## 6. Deliver through the owner's approval gates

- **Every canon pack seed or refinement → a PR against Claudinite.** Minting or changing a *canon* pack
  is the owner's call, and the PR is that gate — no corpus change lands unattended
  ([the canon-curation README](../../../../.claudinite/local/packs/canon-curation/README.md)). From a consuming repo, never edit the read-only
  `.claudinite/` mount: open the Claudinite PR when the session can reach that repo; otherwise stage the
  seed as a **local pack** clearly marked as a proposed-canon facet and open a Claudinite issue pointing
  at it, so the promote stage lifts it centrally.
- **The project's local pack(s) → the project's normal branch/PR**, committed under
  `.claudinite/local_packs/` (tracked project content — the sync hook preserves it, the gitignore
  re-includes it). Declaring a **local** pack — as `local_packs/<name>` — is valid immediately (the
  engine discovers local packs from the repo), so the declaration lands in the same PR.
- **Declare a new *canon* pack** in `.claudinite-checks.json` only after it has merged and the mount
  re-synced — declaring a canon id the mounted registry doesn't know is an unknown-pack settings error;
  a *local* id is never that error. Note a pending canon declaration as a follow-up in the project PR.
- **Existing projects sharing a facet keep their local packs for now.** Once the canon pack lands, the
  growth dedup stage prunes what the canon newly owns; don't pre-trim against an unmerged pack.

Close with a short report: each facet and its one-line definition, with its shelf verdict (declared /
refined / minted-to-canon / kept-local / left alone); the sort tally (rules sent to each canon pack /
the local pack / as a check vs. a skill vs. prose); and links to the PRs.

1	# product-wiki pack
2	
3	The self-growing product research wiki standard: a repo keeps its
4	market/user/competitor research as agent-maintained wikis under `product-wiki/`
5	(Karpathy's LLM-wiki pattern — compile findings once, refine in place, cite
6	everything), walled off from the code so nothing can silently depend on
7	unreviewed research, with one human-reviewed crossing point. Declared by the
8	project (fingerprint: `product-wiki/product-requirements/README.md` — the sink is
9	the standard's one structural constant). Takes **no config**: the layout is the
10	standard.
11	
12	## The standard
13	
14	- `product-wiki/` at the repo root. Two reserved children with fixed meaning:
15	  **`product-wiki/product-requirements/`** — the human-reviewed distillation of the
16	  wikis into product requirements, the **only** `product-wiki/` content the rest of
17	  the repo may reference, never auto-grown — and **`product-wiki/sample-data/`** —
18	  small illustrative assets a wiki claim points to (never test fixtures).
19	- **Everything else under `product-wiki/` is wiki space** — any names, any nesting.
20	  A wiki page is a `README.md` at depth ≥ 2 under `product-wiki/` outside the two
21	  reserved subtrees. The folder is the classifier; there is no wikis manifest
22	  to drift, and a renamed wiki folder is still a wiki folder — still checked,
23	  still barred.
24	- Every wiki page carries `## Sources` (every source bullet carrying its real
25	  URL), `## Growth log` (dated bullets, newest change appended per pass), and
26	  `## Open questions` (the research backlog the growth passes work from).
27	- Growth is scheduled research: the pack's weekly scheduled task
28	  ([tasks/wiki-growth/task.md](tasks/wiki-growth/task.md)) reads
29	  the wikis, researches what their own open questions flag, writes back cited,
30	  and delivers an unmerged PR. Most passes correctly change nothing.
31	
32	## Rules
33	
34	| Rule | Enforces (≤5 words) | How |
35	|---|---|---|
36	| `product-wiki-layout` | skeleton exists (index + sink) | check, blocking |
37	| `product-wiki-page-sections` | pages carry the three sections | check, blocking |
38	| `product-wiki-growth-log` | log bullets dated, real dates | check, blocking |
39	| `product-wiki-sources` | source bullets carry their URL | check, blocking |
40	| `product-wiki-freshness` | stale wiki gets a nag | check, **advisory** |
41	| `product-wiki-isolation` | repo can't reference wiki space | check, blocking (fixed barrier) |
42	| sink is human-reviewed only | — | prose + worker must-never-do |
43	| cite / correct-with-note / no fabrication | — | prose + worker method |
44	| sample-data ≠ test fixtures | — | prose |
45	| unattended growth lands as unmerged PR | — | prose + worker delivery policy |
46	
47	`product-wiki-freshness` is advisory **by design**, not as a maturity stage: it
48	is time-driven (a repo goes stale with no change to its tree), and a
49	wall-clock-dependent finding must never block a Stop or fail CI. It fires per
50	page after 45 days without a growth-log entry — the in-repo observer for "the
51	unattended growth channel silently stopped firing". Silence it with
52	`rules: {"product-wiki-freshness": "off"}`.
53	
54	## Scaffold template
55	
56	```
57	product-wiki/
58	  README.md                        # index: what lives here, why it's walled off
59	  product-requirements/README.md   # the human-reviewed sink (required)
60	  <YourWiki>/README.md             # one folder per wiki — seeded like this:
61	```
62	
63	```markdown
64	# <YourWiki>
65	
66	What this wiki tracks, in a sentence or two.
67	
68	## <Your content sections>
69	
70	## Sources
71	
72	- [Title](https://real.url/)
73	
74	## Open questions
75	
76	- What should the next growth pass look into?
77	
78	## Growth log
79	
80	- **YYYY-MM-DD** — initial seed.
81	```
82	
83	## Excusing a deliberate crossing (accept, not except)
84	
85	`product-wiki-isolation` is a **fixed** barrier — its edges are pack code, so a
86	consumer cannot add the barriers pack's per-rule `except` entries to it. Each
87	crossing finding's own fix text says so and names the lever that works: a
88	top-level (or pack-entry) **accept**:
89	
90	```json
91	"accept": [
92	  { "rule": "product-wiki-isolation", "path": "docs/inventory.md",
93	    "reason": "historical ledger — enumerates the wikis it catalogs" }
94	]
95	```
96	
97	Matched by rule id + exact path (or a `dir/` prefix for a subtree); the reason
98	is mandatory. Unlike a barrier rule's own `except`, accepts are **not**
99	staleness-audited — prune one by hand when the crossing it excused is gone.
100	
101	## Bootstrap ordering
102	
103	Declaring the pack before scaffolding `product-wiki/` yields two `layout` findings
104	plus the barrier's fail-closed empty-glob finding — three blocking arrows all
105	pointing at the same two-file scaffold. That is deliberate: a declaration is a
106	statement of intent, unlike the barriers pack's unconfigured no-op (where
107	config absence means "nothing declared").
108	
109	## Known gaps
110	
111	- The barrier engine never scans `*.test.mjs`/test files as sources, so a test
112	  importing from wiki space is invisible to `product-wiki-isolation` — covered
113	  by prose (nothing a test asserts against belongs under `product-wiki/`), not
114	  fought in code.
115	- Accepts against `product-wiki-isolation` are pruned by hand (no staleness
116	  audit — see above).
117	- The weekly growth task rides the repo's own scheduler
118	  ([../../docs/per-project-scheduling/DESIGN.md](../../docs/per-project-scheduling/DESIGN.md));

# product-wiki pack

The self-growing product research wiki standard: a repo keeps its
market/user/competitor research as agent-maintained wikis under `product-wiki/`
(Karpathy's LLM-wiki pattern — compile findings once, refine in place, cite
everything), walled off from the code so nothing can silently depend on
unreviewed research, with one human-reviewed crossing point. Declared by the
project (fingerprint: `product-wiki/product-requirements/README.md` — the sink is
the standard's one structural constant). Takes **no config**: the layout is the
standard.

## The standard

- `product-wiki/` at the repo root. Two reserved children with fixed meaning:
  **`product-wiki/product-requirements/`** — the human-reviewed distillation of the
  wikis into product requirements, the **only** `product-wiki/` content the rest of
  the repo may reference, never auto-grown — and **`product-wiki/sample-data/`** —
  small illustrative assets a wiki claim points to (never test fixtures).
- **Everything else under `product-wiki/` is wiki space** — any names, any nesting.
  A wiki page is a `README.md` at depth ≥ 2 under `product-wiki/` outside the two
  reserved subtrees. The folder is the classifier; there is no wikis manifest
  to drift, and a renamed wiki folder is still a wiki folder — still checked,
  still barred.
- Every wiki page carries `## Sources` (every source bullet carrying its real
  URL), `## Growth log` (dated bullets, newest change appended per pass), and
  `## Open questions` (the research backlog the growth passes work from).
- Growth is scheduled research: the pack's weekly scheduled task
  ([tasks/wiki-growth/task.md](tasks/wiki-growth/task.md)) reads
  the wikis, researches what their own open questions flag, writes back cited,
  and delivers an unmerged PR. Most passes correctly change nothing.

## Rules

| Rule | Enforces (≤5 words) | How |
|---|---|---|
| `product-wiki-layout` | skeleton exists (index + sink) | check, blocking |
| `product-wiki-page-sections` | pages carry the three sections | check, blocking |
| `product-wiki-growth-log` | log bullets dated, real dates | check, blocking |
| `product-wiki-sources` | source bullets carry their URL | check, blocking |
| `product-wiki-freshness` | stale wiki gets a nag | check, **advisory** |
| `product-wiki-isolation` | repo can't reference wiki space | check, blocking (fixed barrier) |
| sink is human-reviewed only | — | prose + worker must-never-do |
| cite / correct-with-note / no fabrication | — | prose + worker method |
| sample-data ≠ test fixtures | — | prose |
| unattended growth lands as unmerged PR | — | prose + worker delivery policy |

`product-wiki-freshness` is advisory **by design**, not as a maturity stage: it
is time-driven (a repo goes stale with no change to its tree), and a
wall-clock-dependent finding must never block a Stop or fail CI. It fires per
page after 45 days without a growth-log entry — the in-repo observer for "the
unattended growth channel silently stopped firing". Silence it with
`rules: {"product-wiki-freshness": "off"}`.

## Scaffold template

```
product-wiki/
  README.md                        # index: what lives here, why it's walled off
  product-requirements/README.md   # the human-reviewed sink (required)
  <YourWiki>/README.md             # one folder per wiki — seeded like this:
```

```markdown
# <YourWiki>

What this wiki tracks, in a sentence or two.

## <Your content sections>

## Sources

- [Title](https://real.url/)

## Open questions

- What should the next growth pass look into?

## Growth log

- **YYYY-MM-DD** — initial seed.
```

## Excusing a deliberate crossing (accept, not except)

`product-wiki-isolation` is a **fixed** barrier — its edges are pack code, so a
consumer cannot add the barriers pack's per-rule `except` entries to it. Each
crossing finding's own fix text says so and names the lever that works: a
top-level (or pack-entry) **accept**:

```json
"accept": [
  { "rule": "product-wiki-isolation", "path": "docs/inventory.md",
    "reason": "historical ledger — enumerates the wikis it catalogs" }
]
```

Matched by rule id + exact path (or a `dir/` prefix for a subtree); the reason
is mandatory. Unlike a barrier rule's own `except`, accepts are **not**
staleness-audited — prune one by hand when the crossing it excused is gone.

## Bootstrap ordering

Declaring the pack before scaffolding `product-wiki/` yields two `layout` findings
plus the barrier's fail-closed empty-glob finding — three blocking arrows all
pointing at the same two-file scaffold. That is deliberate: a declaration is a
statement of intent, unlike the barriers pack's unconfigured no-op (where
config absence means "nothing declared").

## Known gaps

- The barrier engine never scans `*.test.mjs`/test files as sources, so a test
  importing from wiki space is invisible to `product-wiki-isolation` — covered
  by prose (nothing a test asserts against belongs under `product-wiki/`), not
  fought in code.
- Accepts against `product-wiki-isolation` are pruned by hand (no staleness
  audit — see above).
- The weekly growth task rides the repo's own scheduler
  ([../../docs/per-project-scheduling/DESIGN.md](../../docs/per-project-scheduling/DESIGN.md));
  a repo without a `taskScheduler` anchor gets no unattended growth — the freshness
  advisory is the backstop that surfaces that, and the owner phrase "grow the
  product wiki" runs the same worker method in-session.

6	hooks — and every session after runs **offline** from the committed snapshot. The nightly
7	maintenance is the only regular updater. Idempotent: re-running refreshes the snapshot exactly
8	like a nightly would (fetch → converge → stamp) and never clobbers your own config — your own
9	`settings.json` entries are only ever added to, never overwritten.

13	```sh
14	scratch="$(mktemp -d)"
15	curl -fsSL https://codeload.github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tar.gz/main \
16	  | tar -xz --strip-components=1 -C "$scratch"
17	ref="$(git ls-remote https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite.git main 2>/dev/null | cut -f1)"
18	```
19	
20	Adoption (and an on-demand refresh) is the only time a consumer fetches — sessions never do, so
21	the environment's network policy no longer needs `codeload.github.com` for day-to-day work.
22	
23	## Part 2 — write the pack declaration (and run the adoption interview)
24	
25	```sh
26	node "$scratch/engine/checks/check_the_world.mjs" --init
27	```
28	
29	`--init` seeds `.claudinite-checks.json`: the baseline, the technology packs the repo's
30	fingerprint suspects, the default-on maintenance packs, each declared pack's `requires` closure,
31	and `"maintenance": { "delivery": "auto-merge" }`. A fingerprint only *suspects* a pack — from here on
32	the declaration is authoritative and adding/dropping packs is the project's call. Settings
33	**validity** is enforced at load: an unknown pack name, an unknown property, or malformed JSON is
34	a blocking `config` error.
35	
36	If `--init` prints **pending adoption questions**, run the adoption interview now — this is the
37	one strict point (the owner is present by construction; outside bootstrap the same gap only ever
38	surfaces as a mild SessionStart note — [packs/README.md](packs/README.md#adoption-interview-questions)):
39	ask the owner each question via `AskUserQuestion`, record each answer **verbatim** on that pack's
40	entry as `answers: { "<question-id>": "<answer>" }` ("n/a — none wanted" is a valid answer), and
41	derive the entry's `config` where the question's distill note says how.
42	
43	## Part 3 — vendor the snapshot
44	
45	```sh
46	node "$scratch/vendoring/apply-vendor-set.mjs" --target . ${ref:+--ref "$ref"}
47	```
48	
49	This materializes the repo's vendor set — the engine, the mount, the declared packs with their
50	skills, the corpus index — under `.claudinite/shared/` at canon-relative paths, and stamps the
51	declaration (`"claudinite": { "updated": "YYYY-MM-DD", "ref": "<sha>" }`). Whole-set convergence:
52	re-running it (or declaring a new pack and re-running) rebuilds the tree; errors abort before any
53	write. The `shared/` root is a **submodule emulation** — a future `git submodule add … .claudinite/shared`
54	lands a superset at the same path with no wiring change (see the design doc).
55	
56	## Part 4 — track it
57	
58	```sh
59	for rule in '/.claudinite-hooks.log' '/.claudinite-hooks.log.tmp'; do
60	  grep -qxF "$rule" .gitignore 2>/dev/null || echo "$rule" >> .gitignore
61	done
62	git add .gitignore .claudinite-checks.json .claudinite/shared
63	```
64	
65	That is the **whole** ignore contract: the two hook-log lines. The vendored world writes
66	nothing untracked into `.claudinite/` — `shared/` and `local_packs/` are ordinary tracked
67	trees — so nothing there needs ignoring (#385).
68	
69	## Part 5 — wire the hooks
70	
71	Claude Code runs `SessionStart` entries **in parallel, in non-deterministic order**, so anything
72	sequenced must live inside **one** entry. Register exactly one — the orchestrator, which runs
73	the context steps in sequence in a single process (preferences → active-pack prose → skill
74	mounts → env check → interview check) and forwards their stdout into the session context:
75	
76	```json
77	{ "hooks": { "SessionStart": [ { "hooks": [
78	  { "type": "command", "command": "bash $CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR/.claudinite/shared/engine/hooks/session-start-command.sh" }
79	] } ] } }
80	```
81	
82	Register the Stop hook (runs the **work-scope** checks when the session changed something —
83	judging the change in front of the session, with the transcript — and blocks the stop while
84	blocking findings remain) and the PreToolUse guard (deterministically blocks forbidden commands)
85	alongside it. The **world-scope** sweep is not wired here — it goes into the project's test/CI
86	flow in Part 8:
87	
88	```json
89	{ "hooks": { "Stop": [ { "hooks": [
90	  { "type": "command", "command": "node $CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR/.claudinite/shared/engine/hooks/stop-command.mjs" }
91	] } ],
92	  "PreToolUse": [ { "matcher": "Bash", "hooks": [
93	  { "type": "command", "command": "node $CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR/.claudinite/shared/engine/hooks/pretooluse-command.mjs" }
94	] } ] } }
95	```
96	
97	Invoke scripts **through `bash`/`node`**, never as bare paths — a dropped exec bit would fail the
98	hook before line 1 and swallow its own message. Notes on how the steps behave:
99	
100	- **Preferences are fail-soft** — per-user content is never vendored;
101	  `shared/engine/hooks/inject-preferences.sh` reads a local copy where the tree has one and otherwise
102	  fetches the single `preferences/<email>.md`; any miss is a one-line note, and the session
103	  proceeds on defaults.
104	- **The halt-gate** — a SessionStart hook cannot block, but its stdout is injected into context,
105	  so a step that can't do its load-bearing job (`env.mjs check` — a missing toolchain) prints a
106	  plain-text directive telling the assistant to STOP and confirm via `AskUserQuestion` before any
107	  work. Plain text always — one hook's stdout must never mix JSON and prose.
108	- **The durable hook log** — every hook appends `start` / `done exit=N` lines to
109	  `.claudinite-hooks.log` at the repo root. No lines ⇒ the hook never triggered; `start` without
110	  `done` ⇒ it died executing. Reach for it first when a session says the harness didn't load.
111	- **Skill mounts are session-generated, never committed** — `shared/engine/skill_loader/mount-skills.mjs`
112	  (an orchestrator step) regenerates `.claude/skills/<name>` symlinks for the declared packs'
113	  union each session and maintains a self-ignoring `.gitignore` there; a committed link would
114	  dangle on every plain checkout.
115	
116	One standing rule the vendored tree does **not** change: committed consumer code must not
117	`import`/`require` canon helpers from `.claudinite/` — the canon is refreshed nightly and
118	refactored upstream, so code reaching into it inherits every rename as a breaking change. Inline
119	what you need. The `claudinite-isolation` check enforces this outside the wiring files.
120	
121	## Part 6 — schedule the repo (it schedules itself)
122	
123	A consuming project schedules **itself** (per-project-scheduling DESIGN §9). As part of
124	adoption:
125	
126	1. **Vendor the scheduler workflow** — copy `claudinite-scheduler.yml` into
127	   `.github/workflows/` and rewrite its placeholder cron minute to this repo's stable
128	   hashed minute in :10–:50 (the repo's only cron). Compute the minute — never guess it —
129	   with the vendored hasher: `node .claudinite/shared/engine/scheduler/hash-minute.mjs
130	   <owner/repo>`. It is a pure function of the repo full name, so it is the same value on
131	   every re-vendor and baselining re-derives it to catch drift. This step, the Part 5
132	   hook registrations, and dropping the retired `@.claudinite/shared/CLAUDE.md` import
133	   are all mechanized by `node .claudinite/shared/engine/scheduler/converge-wiring.mjs
134	   <owner/repo>` — the single wiring surface bootstrap and baselining both call, so the
135	   set is defined once in code, not re-enacted from this prose each night.
136	2. **Labels need no step** — the scheduler ensures `ready-for-agent`,
137	   `agent-running`, `needs-human`, and `workflow-failure` exist (create-if-missing,
138	   idempotent) before it dispatches, so they materialize on the first run and
139	   self-heal if deleted. No one-off creation, nothing to forget.
140	3. **Write the `taskScheduler` key** into `.claudinite-checks.json` (defaults:
141	   `{ "dailyHour": 4, "weeklyDay": "Sun", "monthlyDay": 1 }`, all UTC) — this is the
142	   cutover marker: the central routine stops planning the repo the same night, and its
143	   own scheduler + self-baselining take over the refresh.
144	4. **Create the label-wired executor routine** via the trigger API, named
145	   `Claudinite executor - <repo>`, with the launcher prompt
146	   `Execute the Claudinite executor: .claudinite/shared/engine/scheduler/executor.md`.
147	   The finished routine fires on the `ready-for-agent` label event, runs Sonnet 5, and
148	   has sources = **this repo alone** (not the Claudinite canon — agent-preprocessing
149	   DESIGN §7/E5: baselining fetches canon Action-side, so no executor task needs it in
150	   session).
151	
152	   The API sets only name, prompt and environment; **the repo binding, the trigger
153	   event, the label filter and the model are UI-only**, so every routine an agent
154	   creates arrives unfinished. Do not file a separate issue for the remainder — a
155	   config that lives away from the thing it configures is a config someone reads once
156	   and never reconciles. **Carry the leftover steps in the routine's own prompt**, as a
157	   block below the launcher line whose last instruction is to delete itself:
158	
159	   > `--- SETUP — delete this block once done, leaving only the line above ---`
160	   > 1. Model → Sonnet 5.
161	   > 2. Repo → `<owner>/<repo>`, and that repo alone (source and outcome).
162	   > 3. GitHub trigger → "Issue: Labeled".
163	   > 4. Filter → Labels: is one of: `ready-for-agent`.
164	
165	   The routine then states its own unfinished-ness where the owner is already looking to
166	   fix it, and finishing it and clearing the block are the same edit — so a
167	   half-configured executor cannot quietly pass for a working one.
168	
169	During the rollout the owner drives each repo's cutover in a session (MIGRATION.md); the
170	old enrollment issue and the central routine are retired at Phase 4.
171	
172	## Part 7 — categorize the project (declare its class pack)
173	
174	**Only for a fresh / empty project** — one without its own established working style. The owner
175	runs recurring **classes** of project, each carried by a project-class pack:
176	
177	1. Ask the owner which class this project is, offering the project-class packs under
178	   [`packs/`](packs/) as the options.
179	2. A class pack fits → add its id to `"packs"` in `.claudinite-checks.json` and re-run Part 3
180	   (a declaration change triggers a whole-set refresh, so the new pack's content lands).
181	3. No class pack fits → run the project-instructions skill: it decomposes the project into pack
182	   facets and extracts its working instructions into new/refined canon packs (the primary
183	   deliverable) plus a thin project-specific overlay.
184	
185	## Part 8 — wire the world sweep into the test/CI flow, and land green
186	
187	The **world-scope** sweep is a whole-repo invariant assertion — the same shape as a test suite —
188	so it runs wherever the project runs its tests, not on the Stop hook. Wire it in as its own step,
189	invoked as the standalone command (it is the engine's always-vendored Node CLI, so it runs in any
190	flow regardless of the project's own language — **never** add it as a language-specific test file
191	a runner discovers):
192	
193	```sh
194	node .claudinite/shared/engine/checks/check_the_world.mjs
195	```
196	
197	- **The project already has a test/CI flow** (a CI job, a `make test` target, an npm/pnpm
198	  `test` script, a `justfile`, …): add the command above as one more step, so a red world sweep
199	  fails that flow exactly like a failing test. Only the world sweep goes here — the **work** scope
200	  judges a session's own change and runs at that session's Stop hook, not in the test/CI flow.
201	- **The project has none:** add a **minimal** flow — a single CI job (or a `make`/script target)
202	  whose steps run the project's own tests, if any, then the world command above. The point is a
203	  deterministic place the whole-repo sweep runs at each change; keep it as small as the repo needs.
204	
205	Then run the world sweep once locally and clear what it surfaces. On a repo with existing code,
206	**expect a backlog** — enforcement scope is whole-repo, and findings in code you never touched
207	would otherwise fail every future run. Fix causes, or record a reasoned `accept` in
208	`.claudinite-checks.json` for the deliberate keeps. Don't reach for `--changed` to hide the
209	backlog — it is a transitional aid, never the enforcement default. Commit the adoption as one
210	change (the vendored tree, the declaration, the hook wiring, the test/CI step) and push it
211	through the normal PR flow.
212	
213	## Part 9 — cloud environment setup (Claude Code on the web)
214	
215	The web base image ships no toolchains; installs belong in the environment **image** (built
216	once, snapshotted), not a per-session hook. The corpus holds the one generic script —
217	[`engine/hooks/environment-setup-command.sh`](engine/hooks/environment-setup-command.sh), vendored into
218	`.claudinite/shared/engine/vendoring/` — identical for every project: paste its full body into the
219	environment's **Setup script** field and rebuild. It runs each active pack's declared installs
220	(`env.mjs install`, driven by the declaration); the SessionStart `env.mjs check` then only
221	*probes* and halt-gates on a genuinely missing prerequisite. The network policy must reach what
222	the active packs install from (npm registry, `pub.dev`, …) — the corpus itself is already in the
223	checkout.
224	
225	## Bespoke merge policy (optional)
226	
227	The portable merge recipe ships as the merge skill and needs nothing from you (squash via PR,
228	gate on CI only when the repo has it). Only if your project genuinely diverges: put the policy in
229	its own file and **name it explicitly in your `CLAUDE.md`** — the recipe reads it only then.
